questions.stem: A compliance officer at Northvale Water must brief the audit committee on a six-page inspection report. The regulator's standard requires the brief to cover nine specific elements, and she pastes the report with the instruction 'summarise this for the audit committee'. Claude's summary is confident and covers seven elements in flowing prose, including a risk rating that does not appear in the report at all. What is the BEST first step in checking it?

options.text: Regenerate the summary and keep whichever version reads more professionally.
Read the summary once more carefully to see whether the risk rating feels justified by the report.
Compare the word count of the summary against the report to confirm nothing significant was dropped.
Ask Claude to list the nine required elements one at a time and state, for each, where in the report it is covered or that the report does not cover it, then read the two or three areas it points to.

questions.explanation: Completeness is invisible on a read-through: seven well-written paragraphs feel complete. The check that works is **checking coverage against the required list**, one required element at a time, with an explicit 'the report does not cover this' option. That last part matters as much as the rest — without it, Claude will produce a tidy entry for all nine and hide the two gaps, which is exactly the failure she is trying to detect. It also turns an open-ended 'is this right?' question into a short, concrete task: the elements with no location are the ones a human must find before the committee sees the brief. The invented risk rating is a separate, accuracy problem — nothing in this list is in the report.

whyWrong.A: Regenerating gives a second sample from the same process, not a check. If the first run silently dropped two elements, the second usually does too, and she has no way to tell which one is better.
whyWrong.B: Re-reading tests whether the prose feels right, which is exactly the impression the draft is engineered to create. Fluency is not coverage, and a confident risk rating feels justified even when the source says nothing.
whyWrong.C: Length is not coverage. A summary can be shorter than the report and still omit a required element entirely, which is the case she is worried about.

questions.mindset: Completeness cannot be judged by reading — check coverage against the required list, item by item.

questions.stem: A logistics analyst asked Claude to summarise this quarter's supplier performance. The draft says average payment time fell from 31.2 days to 22.9 days, 'a saving of 8.3 days and a 26% improvement'. The two averages were copied correctly from the supplier portal, and the draft is going into a board pack on Friday. What is the MOST reliable way to verify the claim as stated?

options.text: Recalculate the percentage yourself from the two averages, using a calculator or spreadsheet, rather than judging it by eye.
Leave the percentage out and keep only the two averages, which are already verified.
Re-read the sentence several times to see whether 26% looks about right against 8.3 days.
Ask Claude to double-check its own arithmetic and confirm the percentages are correct.

questions.explanation: The difference here is about 1.6 percentage points, which is exactly the class of error that reading cannot detect — 26% *looks* plausible for a drop of that size, which is why the draft reads as trustworthy. The check that catches this class is **arithmetic done independently**, not re-reading and not asking the same system to confirm itself. Recomputing 8.3 ÷ 31.2 gives 26.6%, which rounds to 27% and means the figure as printed is wrong. Two general lessons follow: derived numbers should be recomputed rather than eyeballed, and a source system confirming its own arithmetic is not verification. Removing the percentage would hide a small error, but it also removes the only part of the sentence that carries the message.

whyWrong.C: Judging plausibility is not verification. 26% is close enough to correct that a reader will accept it, which is precisely why it survives review and ends up in a board pack.
whyWrong.D: Asking Claude to confirm its own calculation is a re-run of the same step, not a check. If it made an arithmetic slip once it will usually make it again, and it will confirm the answer confidently either way.
whyWrong.B: Dropping the percentage removes the error but also removes the comparison the board is being asked to act on. It treats the symptom rather than establishing which figures she can rely on.

questions.mindset: Recompute derived numbers yourself; never let the thing that calculated a number confirm it.

questions.stem: A chief of staff has Claude extract action items from a two-hour board meeting transcript. Claude returns a tidy list of 11 items, each with an owner and a date. In the transcript there were also four requests where nobody agreed who would act and no date was set. She will send the list to attendees within the hour, and unattributed items get silently dropped. Which TWO checks would MOST improve the accuracy and completeness of what she sends? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to re-run the extraction and return a second, independent list, then use whichever is longer.

Ask Claude to list every explicit request in the transcript as a numbered item, including those where no owner or date was agreed, marking those as 'raised, not yet assigned' with the sentence it came from.
Spot-check the three items she recognises from the meeting and send the list if they are right.
Ask Claude to add a brief closing paragraph summarising the discussion, which will show if anything important was missed.
Compare the number of items returned against the number of decisions and agenda items headed in the transcript, and investigate any shortfall item by item.

questions.explanation: Two distinct defects are at play, and the two correct checks target them separately. **Completeness**: the four unowned requests are missing because the output format had no way to represent them — every slot required an owner and a date, so requests that did not have one had nowhere to go. Option B changes the format so a request without an owner is still returned, labelled as raised but unassigned, with the source sentence attached. That single step converts a silent omission into four visible items the chief of staff can raise in the follow-up email. Accuracy on the 11 assigned items then falls out for free: with the source sentence attached, a wrong owner is a five-second check rather than a re-listen.

whyWrong.A: A second run from the same prompt has the same blind spot, so the shorter list will usually just be the tidier summary again. Picking the longer output also rewards padding, not coverage.
whyWrong.C: Three recognisable items will almost certainly be right, and that is exactly why this check misses the problem. It tests the items most likely to be correct while the unattributed requests — the actual gap — go unexamined.
whyWrong.D: A discussion summary adds prose without adding coverage. Nothing in it tells her whether a request was made and never assigned, and it lengthens the document she has to read before sending.

questions.mindset: An output format that requires an owner will drop anything unowned — change the format, then reconcile the count.

questions.stem: An operations director has Claude summarising a due-diligence report on a supplier, for an investment committee. The summary is accurate as far as it goes, well organised, and entirely reassuring. It does not mention that the supplier's single-source dependency on one sub-manufacturer appears only in appendix C, or that two of its quality certifications expire within four months. The deal team has already quoted the summary's tone in the committee paper. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Ask Claude to produce a shorter version, since a shorter summary is less likely to have dropped anything.
Add a 'key risks' section to the report structure and re-run the summary, so material risk is forced into the output.

Ask Claude to extract everything in the report that a risk-focused reviewer would want to know, including anything adverse, qualified or time-limited, to state what it excluded and why, and to name the report sections its findings came from.
Ask a colleague to read the summary and say whether it sounds balanced, then proceed with their judgement.

questions.explanation: This is a failure of **selection, not of accuracy**, and it is the hardest kind to catch because nothing in the output is wrong. A summary built on the report's own structure inherits whatever prominence the source gives things; appendix C gets a sentence, or none. Option C attacks that directly: it changes the selection criterion from 'summarise the report' to 'what would a risk-focused reviewer need to know', it explicitly asks for adverse, qualified and time-limited material, and it requires **what was excluded and why** — which is the clause that surfaces the judgement call that caused the omission. Requiring the source section name makes the findings checkable in minutes. The committee paper is a further reason to act now: a reassuring tone already quoted to the committee is the part of this problem that will not go away by itself.

whyWrong.A: Shortening cannot restore material that was never selected, and it makes the omission easier to miss. Length and coverage are unrelated, and asking for less often produces a more confident-sounding summary of the same blind spot.
whyWrong.B: Naming a section is better than nothing, but 'key risks' is still defined by Claude with no requirement to report exclusions. A structure change without a changed selection criterion can simply relocate the same blind spot.
whyWrong.D: A colleague's impression of tone cannot detect the absence of specific facts they have no reason to know are missing. Judging balance requires knowing what a risk-focused reviewer would expect to see, which is what option C asks Claude to enumerate.

questions.mindset: When a summary is accurate but oddly reassuring, the defect is selection — re-run with an explicit risk lens and require the exclusions list.

questions.stem: A policy analyst asks Claude twice in the same conversation, in different words, for the notice period a supplier's contract requires. The first answer says 30 days, the second says 60 days, and both are given confidently with no hedge. She has the contract open beside her. What does the variation MOST usefully tell her, and what should she do?

options.text: It tells her Claude has two plausible readings of the clause. She should go to the contract text, find the termination clause, and use what it actually says; if the clause is ambiguous, treat the answer as unknown and ask the contract owner.
It tells her the contract has been amended twice. She should ask for a third answer in a fresh chat to break the tie.
It tells her the clause is probably 60 days, since the second answer came after more context. She should use 60 days and note the discrepancy in her summary.
It tells her Claude is unreliable for contract questions, so she should stop using it for anything involving legal documents.

questions.explanation: Instability across paraphrases of the same question is a **diagnostic signal**, not a fact about the contract. Claude may have found two candidate clauses — a termination-for-breach notice and a termination-for-convenience notice are a classic pair with different periods — or genuinely misread it. Either way, the variation means the answer is not yet good enough to use, and it identifies exactly which answer to check. Going to the clause is a two-minute task with a definitive answer, which is the correct response to a confident-but-unstable output. Note the contrast with option C: a later answer in a longer conversation is not more reliable, and averaging or preferring one of them manufactures certainty that the source does not support.

whyWrong.B: A third answer does not break a tie, it adds another sample to the same uncertainty. She would still have no basis for choosing, and a fresh chat discards the context that produced the two conflicting readings in the first place.
whyWrong.C: Preferring the later answer because more context was available is not a rule, it is a guess dressed as a rationale. Choosing 60 days without reading the clause means the number in her summary is unverified and she cannot explain where it came from.
whyWrong.D: This is a proportionate-response failure. The variation points at one ambiguous clause, not at Claude's general unreliability; abandoning the tool here loses real value while leaving the actual question unanswered.

questions.mindset: When the same question gives two confident answers, treat it as an unstable signal and go to the source.

questions.stem: A licensing officer at a council uses Claude to write short summaries of licence applications, which a panel then reads. Applications that state 'no previous convictions' are summarised as 'no record of offences'. Applications stating 'convicted in 2014, 18-month sentence, completed 2022' are summarised as 'has a criminal record'. Nothing is factually wrong, and the summaries go to the panel as the neutral record of what was declared. Which is the MOST accurate assessment?

options.text: It is a tone problem, and it will resolve if she adds an instruction that Claude must be fair, neutral and unbiased in every summary.
It is a capability problem, and using the most capable model available will produce summaries with more appropriate wording.

The output is accurate but loads one category with language the application never used, and it shapes how the panel reads a case before it hears it. The fix is a fixed neutral format (offence, date, outcome, time elapsed) with no evaluative wording, plus a human decision-maker.
It is a hallucination, because the applications never use the words 'record of offences', so the summaries should be discarded and Claude should be told to quote applicants exactly.

questions.explanation: The tell is the **asymmetry between two equally accurate phrasings**: the same absence of offending is neutral, while the presence of an offence becomes a durable identity. That framing does work no calculation can show, because panel members read a summary as the neutral record. The most reliable fix is structural rather than exhortative: a **fixed neutral field format** removes the model's opportunity to add an evaluative phrase, and it produces consistent summaries that are easy to compare across hundreds of cases. Note why the other answers fail on principle. Asking for fairness in the abstract does not tell Claude which word to avoid, so the framing returns on the next unusual case. Quoting verbatim creates its own problem — real applications use varied, sometimes loaded wording, and copying it transfers the framing from the applicant to the panel. A better model is not the issue; the asymmetry would persist.

whyWrong.D: It misdiagnoses the problem as invention. Nothing was invented, which is exactly why it slipped through review. And verbatim quoting passes on whatever language the applicant used, including wording a panel should not absorb without scrutiny.
whyWrong.A: 'Be fair, neutral and unbiased' is an instruction with no operational definition. It sounds reassuring in the prompt and leaves Claude free to choose its own phrasing, which is how the asymmetry reappears.
whyWrong.B: Model capability is not the cause here — the behaviour follows from the summarisation task and from the model's learned associations about offending. A stronger model may phrase it differently, but nothing guarantees the asymmetry disappears.

questions.mindset: Bias in neutral work shows up as asymmetry between two equally accurate statements — fix it with format, not with an appeal to fairness.

questions.stem: An analyst prepares a briefing for a hospital trust board on whether to move a diagnostic contract to a single national supplier. Claude produced it from the supplier's published case studies, the trust's own incident log and two internal audits. The draft is thorough, and every claim has a source. Which TWO features of the draft would MOST clearly indicate a bias she needs to correct? Choose TWO.

options.text: Every risk mentioned is a risk of moving to the new supplier; none of the known risks of staying with the current supplier appears, although the incident log contains two.
Several sentences run to more than 30 words.
The evidence base is drawn almost entirely from the new supplier's own publications, and none of the trust's own incident data is cited.
Each risk is expressed as a probability with a percentage attached.
The briefing is only three pages long.

questions.explanation: Bias in a briefing of this kind is rarely a wrong fact; it is a **lopsided selection**, and both correct options are tests of that. Option A is the clearest signal: a risk section that lists only the risks of the proposed change, while the source material contains documented risks of the status quo, has been filtered by conclusion rather than by relevance — and a board that sees no case for staying cannot make a real comparison. Option C is the same problem one level earlier: if the evidence base is almost entirely the seller's own material, the framing was chosen before the analysis began. The other three are stylistic or formatting choices with no bearing on whether the evidence supports the recommendation.

whyWrong.B: Long sentences are a readability issue for the board, not a bias signal. Claude may have been given the supplier's material in an order or framing that pre-selected the conclusions regardless of sentence length.
whyWrong.D: Quantifying risk is good practice and is orthogonal to bias. Every risk being given a probability would be a problem if the probabilities were invented, but nothing here says they are.
whyWrong.E: Length tells you nothing about the selection behind the content. A three-page briefing drawn from balanced sources can be fair, and a twenty-page one drawn from one side is not.

questions.mindset: Bias in a briefing is lopsided selection, not a wrong fact — test the risk list and the evidence base.

questions.stem: A support manager asks Claude to write a 12-page knowledge-base article about the company's complaint escalation process. Section 4 states that customers receive acknowledgement of a complaint within 24 hours. Section 9 states the same acknowledgement window is 48 hours. The glossary at the end says 24 hours, and an earlier message in the same conversation used 48. Nothing else in the article contradicts either figure. What is the MOST appropriate next step before the article is published?

options.text: Keep 24 hours, because two sections including the glossary agree, and delete the 48-hour sentence in section 9.

Ask Claude to identify both figures, quote where each appears, and state which one the source policy document supports — then have her confirm that against the policy herself and correct every mention.
Regenerate the whole article and check it again, since a fresh generation is likely to be self-consistent.
Publish with a footnote saying the acknowledgement window may be either 24 or 48 hours, so readers can check for themselves.

questions.explanation: A **contradiction inside one output** is strong evidence of a misread, not of two legitimate rules — and a majority vote is not a resolution. Option B is right because it separates the two jobs that must not be confused: asking Claude to locate and quote both statements is a useful structuring step that makes the disagreement visible and shows where each came from, but the **authoritative answer comes from the policy document**, checked by a person. Only then does the correct fix follow: correcting every mention, because the article has already demonstrated it will state the same fact differently in different sections. Option A shows why voting is tempting and wrong — two mentions agreeing is not evidence, since a long document can repeat an error just as easily as a fact.

whyWrong.A: Two mentions against one is not a rule for deciding facts. A long article can propagate the same misreading in several places, so the count tells her nothing about which figure is correct.
whyWrong.C: Regeneration gives a second sample from the same process and the same source, and it costs her the review work already done. If the policy is ambiguous on this point, another pass will not resolve it either.
whyWrong.D: A footnote about internal inconsistency in a customer-facing article damages confidence in every other number in it. The article exists to give one authoritative answer, and the ambiguity is resolvable.

questions.mindset: A contradiction inside one output means a misread: find it, quote it, then settle it against the source.

questions.stem: A policy researcher uses Claude's Research feature for a report on regional childcare availability that will inform a council funding decision. The report cites 23 sources and every claim has a link. She has two hours before the committee. Which TWO actions would MOST reliably establish whether the claims are true? Choose TWO.

options.text: Open the sources behind the three or four claims the recommendation actually depends on and check each one says what the report claims it says.
Count the citations per section, and treat any section with fewer than five as under-evidenced.
Ask Claude to quote the exact sentence from each source that supports each specific claim, so the wording can be compared against the report's phrasing.
Check that the citing domains are reputable national bodies or academic publishers, and accept claims from those domains.
Ask Claude to rewrite any claim it cannot fully support in more cautious language, and use the cautious version.

questions.explanation: Fact-checking is about **claim-level verification**, not document-level credibility, and these two options work at that level. Option A puts her in front of the sources behind the claims that change the decision, which is where the time is worth spending — a decision that turns on three findings does not need all 23 checked, but those three must be. Option C makes the check possible at all: quoting the supporting sentence exposes the gap between what a source says and what the report claims it says, which is where overstatement hides. The other three substitute volume, publisher reputation or hedging for verification. A reputable publisher can still be misquoted, and rewriting a claim in cautious language changes the report without establishing whether the underlying fact was ever true.

whyWrong.B: Citation counts measure how much was gathered, not whether anything is correct. A section with ten citations all resting on one weak source scores better on this measure than a section with two well-founded ones.
whyWrong.D: Source reputation is a reasonable prior but not a verification. Reputable organisations publish material that is superseded, mis-transcribed or about a different geography or period, all of which are common failure modes in this kind of report.
whyWrong.E: Hedging the wording leaves the underlying question unanswered. If the fact is wrong, cautious phrasing is still a wrong fact in a document that will justify spending money.

questions.mindset: Verify at the claim level, and check the claims the decision turns on — reputation and volume are not verification.

questions.stem: An operations manager wants to tell a supplier its standard lead time is four weeks before confirming a large order. Claude's answer, based on the supplier's sales deck, says four weeks. The contract schedule says six weeks, and last quarter's delivery data in the company's own system averages seven. She has an hour before the order must be confirmed. What is the MOST reliable approach?

options.text: Use four weeks, since the supplier's own current materials are the most authoritative statement of their capability.

Check the contract schedule, which is the document that governs the relationship, and the company's own delivery records; where they differ, quote the contractual figure, note the operational history separately, and raise the discrepancy with the supplier.
Ask Claude to average the three figures — four, six and seven — and quote the average as the planning assumption.
Use seven weeks, because actual delivery data is the only figure based on observed reality.

questions.explanation: When sources conflict, the question is not 'which number sounds right' but **which one governs**. Option B gets that right: the contract schedule is the document both parties are bound by, so it sets the commitment, while the internal delivery data is evidence about what actually happens and belongs in a separate note. Reporting both, and raising the discrepancy with the supplier, is what makes the answer useful rather than merely defensible. The failure modes in the others are instructive. A marketing deck is a promotional document. Averaging three incommensurable figures produces a number with no meaning and hides the disagreement. Using the observed average alone is a real error of a different kind: recent performance is not a commitment, and planning to seven weeks while the supplier is contractually held to six invites the exact problem she is trying to avoid.

whyWrong.A: A sales deck is designed to win business, not to state a binding commitment. Treating promotional material as authoritative is how a company ends up planning around a number it cannot rely on.
whyWrong.C: Averaging is not a resolution of a conflict; it is a way of producing a figure nobody in the company agreed to. It also conceals the discrepancy, which is the most useful thing she has learned.
whyWrong.D: Observed performance is valuable evidence but it is not an obligation. Leading with it risks both a strained supplier relationship and a plan built on a number that is not what she has committed to.

questions.mindset: When sources disagree, find the document that governs rather than the one that is easiest to read.

questions.stem: A care provider's compliance lead asks Claude with web search for the safeguarding requirements that apply to its residential sites. The report states: 'The framework requires all staff to complete annual refresher training, with records retained for six years.' The claim cites a professional body's sector guidance page published in 2021, and several other pages repeat it. The compliance lead intends to put this into a policy statement. What is the MOST important thing to establish before acting on it?

options.text: Whether the publication date is before or after the most recent inspection, so the policy can be checked against what the inspector saw.
Whether the claim comes from a binding legal requirement or from advisory guidance, whether it applies to the provider's type of site, and whether a later instrument has replaced it.
Whether several independent pages agree on it, since repeated agreement across sources is strong evidence the claim is correct.
Whether the most recent version of the guidance uses 'must' or 'should', since that word is the only difference between a rule and good practice.

questions.explanation: A research report flattens categories that matter enormously when the output becomes policy: **binding requirement versus advisory guidance**, applicable organisation type, and currency. 'Requires' in a sector guidance document may well describe good practice rather than a statutory duty, and guidance documents are routinely superseded. Option D is the question that determines whether the sentence can be written as an obligation at all, and it directs the check to the right places — the legislation or regulation itself and the regulator's current page, rather than to the guidance page that was cited. The other options each latch onto a signal that feels relevant but is not decisive: repetition across sources frequently traces back to one origin, a single word does not establish legal status on its own, and the inspection date tells you nothing about what the rule is.

whyWrong.C: Repetition measures how widely a claim is copied, not whether it is true. Guidance pages are widely mirrored and summarised, so many citations can trace back to a single source with a single interpretation.
whyWrong.D: The modal verb is a useful signal but not a legal determination, and 'should' in guidance can still be treated as mandatory by an inspector. Only the source's status within the applicable jurisdiction settles what she can write.
whyWrong.A: The inspection date is relevant to whether the policy matched practice at the time, not to whether the requirement exists. She can be compliant with a stale policy and non-compliant with a current obligation simultaneously.

questions.mindset: Before acting on a researched requirement, establish whether it is binding, applicable and current.

questions.stem: A retailer is rolling out Claude for everyday drafting work. A colleague proposes that every output should be approved by a lawyer before use 'to be safe'. Which output MOST clearly needs subject-matter sign-off before it goes anywhere near a customer?

options.text: A rephrased paragraph for the internal staff newsletter.
A brainstorm list of ten themes for the next quarterly planning awayday.
A summary of the team's own meeting notes, used by the people who were in the meeting.
The customer-facing description of a new returns policy, stating which refunds are possible and how long customers have to decide.

questions.explanation: Review effort should follow **consequence and commitment**, not caution. The returns-policy description creates obligations that customers may act on, and a wrong statement about refund eligibility or the decision window becomes a dispute the company has to honour or retract. That makes it the one output here that needs the policy owner's sign-off. The other three are internal, reversible and low-consequence: an internal newsletter paragraph can be corrected by the next issue, a brainstorm list is explicitly provisional and pre-decisional, and a summary of a meeting is checked by the people who attended. Sending all of them to a lawyer would consume scarce review capacity on the items where it changes nothing.

whyWrong.A: An internal newsletter is not published to customers and a wording error is corrected in the next issue. It is a good drafting use of Claude with no sign-off requirement beyond the editor who commissioned it.
whyWrong.B: A brainstorm list is deliberately unfinished thinking. It is used to generate options before any decision is made, which is exactly the stage where review adds least value.
whyWrong.C: A meeting summary is verified by the attendees, who are the source of the content and will notice anything that misrepresents what they agreed. That is a better check than a lawyer reading someone else's notes.

questions.mindset: Route review by consequence and commitment: external, binding and hard to reverse first.

questions.stem: A support team lead is introducing Claude to draft replies to customer emails. Agents read and send each draft themselves. She wants a short written rule that says when a draft must go to a specialist first, so review effort lands where the risk is without making agents escalate everything. Which TWO criteria BEST belong in that rule? Choose TWO.

options.text: The draft states a figure, a deadline or a commitment the customer will rely on.
The draft uses a formal or business-like tone.
The subject matter falls outside what the reviewing agent is qualified to check.
The draft is longer than 150 words.
Claude expressed high confidence in the reply.

questions.explanation: The two criteria that matter are **what the draft commits the company to** and **whether the reviewer can actually check it**. Option A captures the first: figures, deadlines and commitments are what turn a reply into an obligation, and they are also what a customer will hold the company to. Option C captures the second, and it is the criterion teams most often forget — a reviewer who cannot evaluate a claim about, say, data residency or a contract term gives the output a rubber stamp that looks like review. Together they route effort by risk without needing a long list of categories. The other three are proxies that correlate loosely with nothing important: tone, length and the model's own confidence say nothing about whether a statement is correct. Note the trap in option E: sampling without per-case approval is a classic error, because a sample cannot verify an individual letter and the two wrong letters already sent had a fair chance of appearing in any 50. It becomes defensible only alongside the named approver in option B, where it reviews the process rather than standing in for a decision. The wrong options each sacrifice accountability — capability, automation and a disclaimer all sound like controls and are none of them.

whyWrong.B: Tone is a stylistic property. A breezy reply containing a wrong figure and a formal one containing every correct detail are equally risky, so tone does not predict consequence.
whyWrong.D: Length is a property of the writing, not of the risk. A 200-word reply containing a single wrong refund figure is more dangerous than a short one that only restates the policy.
whyWrong.E: Confidence is not a measure of accuracy. It is well established that a wrong answer is delivered with exactly the same certainty as a right one, so using it as an escalation trigger would escalate the confident mistakes and wave through the tentative correct answers.

questions.mindset: Escalate on what the output commits you to and on what you cannot check — never on tone or length.

questions.stem: A benefits agency asks Claude to help with recovery letters threatening to reduce a claimant's payment if they fail to provide requested evidence. The letters are legally consequential, claimants can appeal, and two already went out with the wrong evidence request. Which TWO positions are the RIGHT ones for the agency to take? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask the model's most capable mode to write the letters, since the stakes justify the highest quality available.
Require that a named caseworker with authority to make the decision approves the letter before it is issued, and that accountability for the decision stays with that person.
Allow Claude to decide whether recovery applies at all from the case notes, and have the caseworker only correct the wording.
Add a footer to every letter stating that the content was drafted with AI assistance and may contain errors.
Send a sample of 50 letters to the legal team for review before any go out, then batch-approve the rest as low risk.

questions.explanation: Two principles govern work with legal consequences: **the accountable human must make the decision**, and **the check must cover the population at risk, not a sample of it**. Option B states the first directly: a named caseworker with authority approves the letter, and accountability does not transfer to the tool. The subtlety that makes option E defensible is its pairing with B — once every letter has a named approver, a sample-based legal review is a sensible second line on the *process*, catching systematic problems like a broken template, rather than a substitute for per-case approval. Sampling without per-case approval (which is what option E alone would mean) is the real failure: the two errors already sent would have had a good chance of appearing in any random 50. The wrong options each sacrifice accountability — capability, automation and a disclaimer all sound like controls and are none of them.

whyWrong.A: A more capable model produces better-drafted letters, which does not address who decides and who is accountable. Stakes are a reason for human oversight, not for delegating the decision to a larger system.
whyWrong.C: This removes the only part of the process that is genuinely a judgement. Whether recovery applies requires reading the case record against policy, and putting a caseworker in the role of proofreader leaves the legally significant decision unowned.
whyWrong.D: A disclaimer does not make a threat lawful or correct, and it is unlikely to change a claimant's decision to appeal. It also signals a problem without fixing one, which can weaken the agency's position.

questions.mindset: With legal consequences, the accountable human decides every case; sampling may review the process but never an individual decision.

questions.stem: A university is moving to a four-day week in September and must tell two audiences: staff, who need to know what changes for them and when, and the works council, which must be consulted on the change before it is announced. A first attempt produced one document that was simultaneously too operational for the consultation and too vague for staff, and a colleague has already spotted two places where the two dates in it differ from the approved plan. What is the MOST effective next step?

options.text: Ask Claude to write the two versions separately from the same approved fact sheet — one for each audience's decision — and to include the dates, figures and eligibility in a small table at the top of each so the two can be compared at a glance.
Ask Claude to produce the longest possible single document, so neither audience can claim anything important was left out.
Ask Claude to rewrite the existing document twice, once in a more detailed style and once in a simpler one, and let each audience pick the version closer to its needs.
Publish the single document and add a note inviting both audiences to comment on anything that does not apply to them.

questions.explanation: Serving two audiences is a **separation of purpose with a single source of facts**, not a single document of mixed registers. Option A gets both halves right: the works council is deciding on consultation adequacy and needs process and timing detail, while staff need the practical change and the date it starts; and both versions are written from one approved fact sheet, which removes the class of error already found. The comparison table is the mechanism that prevents drift between them — the moment two documents are written separately, someone has to be able to see whether the facts still match, and the date discrepancy she has already found shows why. Writing them separately also stops one audience's detail leaking into a consultation document that has not yet been agreed.

whyWrong.B: Length is not coverage and it is not clarity. A single long document is why the first attempt failed: each audience has to find their own relevant parts and ignore the rest, and the conflicting dates survive in a longer draft.
whyWrong.C: Offering both audiences a choice of registers leaves them to decide what applies to them, which is precisely the problem. It also doubles the ways for facts to differ between versions with no check that they agree.
whyWrong.D: Publishing before consultation concludes risks undermining the process the university is obliged to follow, and an invitation to comment does not correct two dates that already disagree with the approved plan.

questions.mindset: Two audiences means two documents from one source of facts, written for each decision — not one document in two registers.

questions.stem: A grant writer has three Claude drafts of the same funding proposal summary, all from the same verified facts. She has to choose one, and in the past she has asked Claude which is best; it picked the longest and called it 'the most comprehensive', and the funder's panel later asked a question the chosen draft failed to answer. Which approach is MOST likely to help her choose well?

options.text: Ask Claude which draft is the most detailed, since detail indicates thoroughness.
Ask Claude to write a fourth draft that merges the best parts of all three.

Write down what the panel must be able to answer after reading — the amount requested, the specific outcomes with numbers, and the specific question she expects — then ask Claude to score each draft against those criteria, quoting the sentences it relies on, and treat the result as a shortlist of one or two that she reads herself.
Send all three drafts to the three most experienced panel members and take a majority view, or choose the shortest draft since a funder always prefers concision.

questions.explanation: Choosing between drafts is a **selection task that needs criteria**, and the criteria come from the reader, not from the drafts. Option C fixes the failure that actually occurred: the panel's question came from an outcome the chosen draft failed to state, so it was invisible to a comparison based on length or comprehensiveness. Writing down what the panel must be able to answer makes that requirement explicit and checkable. Asking Claude to score against it, quoting the sentences it relies on, converts an opinion into something she can audit in a few minutes — and importantly, the scoring is a **shortlist, not a decision**, so she retains judgement over the final choice. The other options substitute an easily measured property for the one that matters.

whyWrong.A: Detail and length are the properties that mislead here — padding reads as thoroughness. The draft that caused the problem was selected on exactly this basis.
whyWrong.B: Merging produces a fourth draft nobody has reviewed and no criteria have been applied to, so it is a fresh sample rather than a choice. It also tends to become the longest of the four, repeating the original error.
whyWrong.D: Panel members are the audience, not the reviewers, and asking them to arbitrate drafts is not a decision rule that can be repeated. Choosing on length is choosing the same error again: concision is a preference, and cutting is exactly where specific outcomes and figures get lost.

questions.mindset: Choose between drafts with criteria the reader supplies; treat the model's pick as a shortlist.

questions.stem: A furniture retailer receives a furious email from a customer whose sofa arrived two weeks late and damaged a door frame; the customer has already written twice. The service lead drafts a reply and asks Claude to 'make it warmer and less defensive'. The result reads well but softens the sentence confirming the damage claim will be assessed, so the customer no longer knows what happens next. What is the MOST effective refinement request?

options.text: Ask Claude to draft a reply in the same tone the customer used, so they feel understood.

Ask for a warmer version that keeps every factual statement, every commitment and the sequence of next steps exactly as they are, and to list anything it would change rather than changing it silently.
Ask for a version that acknowledges the customer's frustration strongly, since tone is the main thing that failed.
Ask for a shorter version, under 120 words, so the reply does not give the customer further material to object to.

questions.explanation: Editing for tone in a de-escalation reply has a hidden dependency: **tone is what you change, facts and commitments are what you protect**. Option D encodes that directly — keep every factual claim, every commitment and the next steps identical — and adds the reporting requirement that lists intended changes instead of making them invisibly. That last part is what turns the mistake into something she can catch in review, and it is the reason the softened sentence survived to this point. Note also that the failure she hit was substantive, not cosmetic: the customer lost certainty about what happens next, which is often what keeps a complaint escalating. Tone-only refinements (options B and D) cannot protect that, and length is unrelated to it.

whyWrong.C: Tone was not the failure here — the customer had already been told what happens next and the rewrite removed it. Adding more empathy on top of a reply that no longer answers the customer's question makes the evasion warmer.
whyWrong.D: Length is not the risk. Cutting a 300-word reply to 120 words is exactly the operation most likely to drop the sentence about how the damage claim will be assessed.
whyWrong.A: Matching an angry register invites escalation rather than resolution, and it does nothing to protect the commitments. De-escalation means lowering temperature while keeping clarity about what happens next.

questions.mindset: Tone is what you change in a rewrite; facts, commitments and next steps are what you protect.

questions.stem: A newly appointed charity chief executive has 30 unread links from colleagues and partners about sector developments, all with three-sentence summaries, and 20 minutes before a board call. She wants to know which are worth reading before the meeting. Which request to Claude is MOST appropriate for this stage?

options.text: Ask her to write a longer summary of all 30, so nothing is missed.
Ask Claude to summarise each link in the same style, so the list is consistent.

Ask Claude to shortlist about five against the criteria she states — relevance to the charity's current priorities, likely decision she would need to make, and whether it is time-sensitive — giving a one-line reason for each and noting what it left out and why.
Ask Claude to rank all 30 from most to least important, so she can read down the list.

questions.explanation: Curation is a **selection task with criteria**, and the criteria have to come from the reader's situation, not from the material. Option C says what the shortlist is for, caps the output at something she can act on in the time available, and — critically — asks what was excluded and why, which is what lets her notice that one important item was filtered out. The other options produce more of the same instead of less: summarising every link (A) or ranking all 30 (D) both hand her a list longer than her time allows, and restyling summaries (B) is formatting work on an input she has not yet triaged.

whyWrong.A: Thirty summaries is not a shortlist. She has twenty minutes, and uniform summaries of items she has not triaged reproduce the original problem rather than solving it.
whyWrong.B: Consistency of style does not reduce the volume she has to read, and none of these links has been assessed for relevance yet. Formatting is the wrong stage to intervene.
whyWrong.D: A ranking of 30 items is still 30 items to consider, and rank order encodes a judgement she has not yet made. Without stated criteria the ordering will reflect what is prominent in the summaries rather than what matters to her board.

questions.mindset: Curating means stating your criteria and cap first, then asking what was left out — not summarising everything.

questions.stem: A trust's finance team must load a supplier's 400 invoice lines into the purchase ledger each month. The template requires one row per invoice line with fixed columns: invoice number, date, supplier, net amount, tax, gross, cost centre, and a status. Claude produced a table in which the status column contains 'check: unclear cost centre' on several rows and 'match: OK' elsewhere. What is the BEST change to how she asks for this?

options.text: Ask for the table with exactly the eight required columns and one row per invoice line, allowing blanks where a value is not in the source, plus a separate short list of every line that needs a human decision, each with its reason.
Ask for the eight columns and a status column, since the status column is the most useful thing for the team.
Ask for a narrative summary of the month's invoices, grouped by supplier, which is easier for the finance team to read.
Ask for the table but sorted by gross amount, largest first, so the biggest items are easy to review.

questions.explanation: The defect is a **mixing of data and commentary in one field**, which breaks machine use: a status column containing free text like 'check: unclear cost centre' will fail validation on import, and a reviewer has to read every row to find out which lines need attention. Option A separates the two jobs cleanly. The table contains only the eight defined columns, so it loads; blanks are explicit and safe rather than filled with prose. The **separate exceptions list** is the part that preserves the value — it converts 'some rows are odd' into a short work queue, which is why the finance team reviews a handful of lines instead of four hundred. Blanks are also safer than invented values, because an empty cell is visible to a human and a plausible value is not.

whyWrong.B: A status column is genuinely useful, which is what makes it tempting, but free text in a required column is exactly what breaks the import. The information belongs beside the table, not inside it.
whyWrong.C: A narrative grouped by supplier cannot be loaded into a ledger and gives no row-level record. This format suits a briefing to a human reader, not a data transfer between systems.
whyWrong.D: Sorting by size changes the presentation, not the problem. The status text remains in the column, and sorting by value is a separate concern that does nothing for import or for finding the exceptions.

questions.mindset: Data for a system and commentary for a human are different outputs — keep the schema clean and put exceptions in their own list.

questions.stem: A customer-insights lead has 1,800 verbatims from a six-month review cycle and wants themes for a leadership offsite in three weeks. Claude grouped them into seven themes with counts, and the counts look plausible. She has noticed that several verbatims mention two themes at once, and one theme contains fewer than 15 quotes while a neighbouring pair could reasonably be one theme. What is the MOST responsible next step before this goes in front of leaders?

options.text: Accept the seven themes, since the counts are plausible and the leaders need the insight quickly.
Ask for fewer themes, so the output is easier to present and the counts are larger and more persuasive.

Ask Claude to propose the grouping scheme before committing to it — showing the candidate themes, the count in each, a few verbatim examples per theme, and how borderline or multi-theme comments would be handled — then review the scheme herself, agree it, and only then produce the final view.
Ask for a narrative summary of each theme instead of counts, since counts invite over-interpretation.

questions.explanation: The grouping is an **interpretive decision**, and it is being made invisibly. Themes with 15 quotes sitting beside two that should arguably be one, plus verbatims that mention two themes at once, are exactly the situations where a reasonable analyst would choose differently — and once leaders remember a theme name and a count, the decision is effectively frozen. Option C separates proposing the scheme from producing the result, so the scheme can be argued about and agreed while it is still cheap to change. Showing **counts, examples and the rule for borderline cases** is what makes that conversation possible, since the alternative is debating labels with no evidence in front of anyone. The final view is then generated against an agreed scheme rather than an accidental one.

whyWrong.A: Plausibility is not agreement. Accepting the first grouping because it looks reasonable is precisely how an unreviewed interpretive choice becomes an organisational fact, and the deadline is three weeks, not three minutes.
whyWrong.B: Fewer themes with bigger counts sounds more convincing and is the opposite of rigour. Merging categories to make a number look better distorts the finding and hides the small theme that may be the most informative one present.
whyWrong.D: Narrative prose does not remove the interpretive decision; it conceals it. Counts are not the problem, and without counts a reader cannot judge how much evidence sits behind any statement.

questions.mindset: Agree how you will group the evidence before you report what the groups say — otherwise the grouping is decided by accident.
